```{r as-style, include=FALSE}
# ---- Presentation: 95% confidence intervals instead of significance stars ----
# These local definitions override the shared helpers for this paper only (R/helpers.R is untouched).
stars <- function(p) ""
# Never print a negative zero ("-0.0", "-0.00"); otherwise as the shared helper.
# Round half-up in steps (3 -> 2 -> d decimals), so a number in the text always equals the
# table's 2- or 3-decimal value rounded to the text's precision.
.rhu <- function(x, d) sign(x) * floor(abs(x) * 10^d + 0.5 + 1e-9) / 10^d
.fmt <- function(x, d, suffix = "") {
  x <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x)); x[!is.finite(x)] <- NA
  if (d < 3) { x <- .rhu(x, 3); for (k in seq(2, d)) x <- .rhu(x, k) }
  s <- sub("^-(0\\.?0*)$", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ","))
  ifelse(is.na(x), "--", paste0(s, suffix))
}
f3 <- function(x) .fmt(x, 3)
ci_txt <- function(lo, hi, d = 1) paste0("CI ", .fmt(lo, d), " to ", .fmt(hi, d))
est_se <- function(e, digits = 1, unit = "minutes") {
  if (is.null(e$est) || is.na(e$est)) return("not estimable")
  paste0(.fmt(e$est, digits), if (nzchar(unit)) paste0(" ", unit) else "",
         " (", ci_txt(e$est - 1.96 * e$se, e$est + 1.96 * e$se, digits), ")")
}
diff_txt <- function(e, more = "more", less = "less", digits = 1, unit = "minutes") {
  if (is.null(e$est) || is.na(e$est)) return("[not estimable]")
  paste0(.fmt(abs(e$est), digits), if (nzchar(unit)) paste0(" ", unit) else "", " ", more_less(e$est, more, less),
         " (", ci_txt(e$est - 1.96 * e$se, e$est + 1.96 * e$se, digits), ")")
}
diff_pp <- function(e, more = "higher", less = "lower", digits = 1) {
  if (is.null(e$est) || is.na(e$est)) return("not estimable")
  paste0(.fmt(100 * abs(e$est), digits), " percentage points ", more_less(e$est, more, less),
         " (", ci_txt(100 * (e$est - 1.96 * e$se), 100 * (e$est + 1.96 * e$se), digits), ")")
}
# A weighted mean with its standard error, as printed in the tables.
est_m <- function(e, digits = 1) paste0(.fmt(e$est, digits), " minutes (SE ", .fmt(e$se, digits), ")")
ci_cell <- function(k, d = 2) if (is.null(k$est) || is.na(k$est)) "--" else
  paste0("[", .fmt(k$est - 1.96 * k$se, d), ", ", .fmt(k$est + 1.96 * k$se, d), "]")
nw <- function(n) { w <- c("zero", "one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight", "nine", "ten")
  n <- suppressWarnings(as.integer(n)); if (length(n) == 1 && !is.na(n) && n >= 0 && n <= 10) w[n + 1] else .fmt(n, 0) }
```

```{r sample}
R <- CODE$relation
HEADLVL <- unname(R[c("head", "spouse")])
JUNIOR  <- unname(R[c("married_child", "child_spouse")])
PARENT  <- unname(R["parent_or_inlaw"])

# ---- Household-level counts (added to pd BEFORE any subsetting) ----------------
hhx <- pd[, .(
  n_junior_mw  = sum(female == 1 & married == 1 & rel %in% JUNIOR & age >= 15 & age <= 49),
  n_head_mw    = sum(female == 1 & married == 1 & rel %in% HEADLVL & age >= 18 & age <= 49),
  n_mw_18_49   = sum(female == 1 & married == 1 & age >= 18 & age <= 49),
  n_adult_women = sum(female == 1 & age >= 15),
  hh_cc_all    = sum(care_child[age >= 15])
), by = hh_id]
pd[hhx, on = "hh_id", names(hhx)[-1] := mget(paste0("i.", names(hhx)[-1]))]

# ---- Candidate mothers ----------------------------------------------------------
# Married women 18-49 whose roster position identifies the generation above them.
elig0 <- pd[female == 1 & married == 1 & age >= 18 & age <= 49 & rel %in% c(HEADLVL, JUNIOR)]
elig0[, junior := as.integer(rel %in% JUNIOR)]
# A head-level woman who lives with a married child's couple of childbearing age is,
# in a household with a child under six, most likely that child's grandmother rather
# than its mother. She is excluded from the mother sample and enters the
# older-generation sample below.
n_u6_pool   <- elig0[!is.na(hh_n_under6) & hh_n_under6 > 0, .N]
n_u6_dropgm <- elig0[!is.na(hh_n_under6) & hh_n_under6 > 0 & junior == 0 & n_junior_mw > 0, .N]
elig <- elig0[!(junior == 0 & n_junior_mw > 0)]

# ---- Link each mother to the older generation's own diaries -----------------------
older <- pd[, .(hh_id, o_pid = pid, o_rel = rel, o_female = female, o_age = age,
                o_cc = care_child, o_cc_act = care_child_active, o_cc_pas = care_child_passive,
                o_dom = unpaid_domestic, o_emp = employment, o_ft = free_time,
                o_employed = employed)]
lk <- rbind(
  merge(elig[junior == 0, .(pid, hh_id)], older[o_rel == PARENT], by = "hh_id", allow.cartesian = TRUE),
  merge(elig[junior == 1, .(pid, hh_id)], older[o_rel %in% HEADLVL & o_age >= 40], by = "hh_id",
        allow.cartesian = TRUE))
n_self_links <- lk[o_pid == pid, .N]          # must be 0: no mother is her own grandmother
lk <- lk[o_pid != pid]
og <- lk[, .(
  gm_n = sum(o_female == 1), gf_n = sum(o_female == 0),
  gm_care_child = sum(o_cc * (o_female == 1)), gm_cc_act = sum(o_cc_act * (o_female == 1)),
  gm_cc_pas = sum(o_cc_pas * (o_female == 1)), gm_domestic = sum(o_dom * (o_female == 1)),
  gm_employment = sum(o_emp * (o_female == 1)), gm_free_time = sum(o_ft * (o_female == 1)),
  gm_employed = as.integer(any(o_female == 1 & o_employed %in% 1)),
  gm_age_min = if (any(o_female == 1)) min(o_age[o_female == 1]) else NA_real_,
  gf_care_child = sum(o_cc * (o_female == 0))
), by = pid]

Mo <- merge(elig, og, by = "pid", all.x = TRUE)
zero <- c("gm_n", "gf_n", "gm_care_child", "gm_cc_act", "gm_cc_pas", "gm_domestic",
          "gm_employment", "gm_free_time", "gm_employed", "gf_care_child")
for (v in zero) Mo[is.na(get(v)), (v) := 0]
# Agreement with the shared panel's count of older-generation women (should be 100%).
share_link_consistent <- Mo[, mean(gm_n == n_older_gen_women, na.rm = TRUE)]

Mo[, `:=`(
  gm_any   = as.integer(gm_n > 0),
  gf_any   = as.integer(gf_n > 0),
  gp_any   = as.integer(gm_n + gf_n > 0),
  husband  = as.integer(!is.na(spouse_pid)),
  spouse_emp = fifelse(is.na(spouse_employed), 0L, as.integer(spouse_employed)),
  father_cc = fifelse(is.na(spouse_care_child), 0, spouse_care_child),
  special  = as.integer(special_care %in% CODE$yes_no["yes"]),
  kids_6_17 = fcoalesce(as.integer(own_kids_6_17), 0L),
  kids_unknown = as.integer(is.na(own_kids_6_17)),
  sole     = as.integer(n_mw_18_49 == 1),
  any_cc   = as.integer(care_child > 0),
  edu_hi   = as.integer(edu_tier %in% names(CODE$edu_tier)[3:4])
)]
Mo[, spouse_edu_f := factor(fifelse(husband == 0, "No linked husband",
                                    fifelse(is.na(spouse_edu_tier), "Unknown", as.character(spouse_edu_tier))))]
Mo[, `:=`(
  gm_only = as.integer(gm_any == 1 & gf_any == 0),
  gf_only = as.integer(gm_any == 0 & gf_any == 1),
  gp_both = as.integer(gm_any == 1 & gf_any == 1),
  gm_young = as.integer(gm_any == 1 & gm_age_min < 60),
  gm_old   = as.integer(gm_any == 1 & gm_age_min >= 60),
  gm_work  = as.integer(gm_any == 1 & gm_employed == 1),
  gm_nowork = as.integer(gm_any == 1 & gm_employed == 0),
  n_other_women = pmax(n_adult_women - 1 - gm_n, 0),
  hh_care_mo_gm = care_child + gm_care_child,
  others_cc = pmax(hh_cc_all - care_child - father_cc - gm_care_child - gf_care_child, 0),
  gp_lab = factor(ifelse(gm_any == 1, "Grandmother present", "No grandmother"),
                  levels = c("No grandmother", "Grandmother present"))
)]

MY <- Mo[!is.na(hh_n_under6) & hh_n_under6 > 0]                     # analysis sample
MP <- Mo[!is.na(hh_n_under6) & hh_n_under6 == 0 & !is.na(youngest_own_kid) &
           youngest_own_kid >= 6 & youngest_own_kid <= 14]           # placebo sample
MY[, multi_u6 := as.integer(hh_n_under6 >= 2)]

# ---- Specification ----------------------------------------------------------------
CV <- c("i(age_band)", "i(edu_tier)", "urban", "i(mpce_quintile)", "kids_6_17", "kids_unknown",
        "hh_n_under6", "hh_n_6_14", "i(spouse_edu_f)", "spouse_emp", "i(social_group_f)",
        "i(religion_f)", "special", "proxy_report")
f <- function(y, x = "gm_any", d = MY, extra = NULL)
  reg(as.formula(paste(y, "~", x, "+", ctrl(d, c(CV, extra)), fe(d))), d)

# Difference between two coefficients of one model, with SE.
dcoef <- function(m, a, b) {
  if (is.null(m) || !all(c(a, b) %in% names(coef(m)))) return(list(est = NA, se = NA, p = NA))
  v <- vcov(m); d <- unname(coef(m)[a] - coef(m)[b])
  s <- sqrt(v[a, a] + v[b, b] - 2 * v[a, b]); list(est = d, se = s, p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(d / s)))
}
cell <- function(k, d = 2) .fmt(k$est, d)
# Difference of estimates from two separate regressions; SE ignores their covariance
# (conservative when the covariance is positive, as within households and FSUs).
ddiff <- function(a, b) {
  if (is.na(a$est) || is.na(b$est)) return(list(est = NA, se = NA, p = NA))
  d <- a$est - b$est; s <- sqrt(a$se^2 + b$se^2); list(est = d, se = s, p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(d / s)))
}
cse  <- function(k, d = 2) if (is.null(k$est) || is.na(k$est)) "--" else
  paste0(.fmt(k$est, d), " ", ci_cell(k, d))

outs <- c("care_child", "care_child_active", "care_child_passive", "sec_care_child",
          "unpaid_domestic", "dom_food", "care_dep_adult", "employment", "free_time", "sleep")
out_lab <- c(care_child = "Childcare (primary)", care_child_active = "\\quad Active childcare",
             care_child_passive = "\\quad Passive childcare (minding)",
             sec_care_child = "Childcare as secondary activity", unpaid_domestic = "Unpaid domestic work",
             dom_food = "\\quad of which food and meals", care_dep_adult = "Care of dependent adults",
             employment = "Employment (incl. travel)", free_time = "Free time", sleep = "Sleep",
             employed = "Employed (usual status, share)")
m_gm <- setNames(lapply(c(outs, "employed"), f), c(outs, "employed"))
e <- function(y, t = "gm_any", ml = m_gm) coef_of(ml[[y]], t)

k_cc <- e("care_child"); k_act <- e("care_child_active"); k_pas <- e("care_child_passive")
k_sec <- e("sec_care_child"); k_dom <- e("unpaid_domestic"); k_food <- e("dom_food")
k_adult <- e("care_dep_adult"); k_emp <- e("employment"); k_ft <- e("free_time")
k_sleep <- e("sleep"); k_lfp <- e("employed")
k_all <- coef_of(f("hh_cc_all"), "gm_any")
k_fa  <- coef_of(f("father_cc", d = MY[husband == 1]), "gm_any")

# ---- Descriptives -----------------------------------------------------------------
n_my <- nrow(MY); n_mp <- nrow(MP)
share_gm  <- wmean(MY$gm_any, MY$weight)
share_gf  <- wmean(MY$gf_any, MY$weight)
share_gfo <- wmean(MY$gf_only, MY$weight)
share_jun <- wmean(MY$junior, MY$weight)
share_dil <- if (nrow(MY[junior == 1])) wmean(MY[junior == 1]$rel == R["child_spouse"], MY[junior == 1]$weight) else NA
share_jun_gm <- if (nrow(MY[gm_any == 1])) wmean(MY[gm_any == 1]$junior, MY[gm_any == 1]$weight) else NA
share_hus <- wmean(MY$husband, MY$weight)
share_sole <- wmean(MY$sole, MY$weight)
n_jun_nogm <- MY[junior == 1 & gm_any == 0, .N]; n_jun_gm <- MY[junior == 1 & gm_any == 1, .N]
n_head_nogm <- MY[junior == 0 & gm_any == 0, .N]; n_head_gm <- MY[junior == 0 & gm_any == 1, .N]
mo_cc0 <- est_mean(MY[gm_any == 0], "care_child"); mo_cc1 <- est_mean(MY[gm_any == 1], "care_child")
gm_cc  <- est_mean(MY[gm_any == 1], "gm_care_child")
gm_dom <- est_mean(MY[gm_any == 1], "gm_domestic")
gm_empm <- est_mean(MY[gm_any == 1], "gm_employment")
gm_age_med <- if (nrow(MY[gm_any == 1])) median(MY[gm_any == 1]$gm_age_min) else NA
share_gm_young <- if (nrow(MY[gm_any == 1])) wmean(MY[gm_any == 1]$gm_young, MY[gm_any == 1]$weight) else NA
emp_cell <- function(j, g) { d <- MY[junior == j & gm_any == g]; c(sh = wmean(d$employed, d$weight), mn = wmean(d$employment, d$weight)) }
EC <- list(h0 = emp_cell(0, 0), h1 = emp_cell(0, 1), j0 = emp_cell(1, 0), j1 = emp_cell(1, 1))
share_gm_work <- if (nrow(MY[gm_any == 1])) wmean(MY[gm_any == 1]$gm_work, MY[gm_any == 1]$weight) else NA
gm_share_cc <- with(MY[gm_any == 1], sum(weight * gm_care_child) / sum(weight * (gm_care_child + care_child)))

# ---- Heterogeneity ------------------------------------------------------------------
MIN_CELL <- 30   # minimum mothers with and without a grandmother for a split to be reported
het <- function(d, y = "care_child") {
  ok <- d[gm_any == 1, .N] >= MIN_CELL && d[gm_any == 0, .N] >= MIN_CELL
  if (!ok) return(list(est = NA, se = NA, p = NA, n = nrow(d), ok = FALSE))
  c(coef_of(f(y, d = d), "gm_any"), n = nrow(d), ok = TRUE)
}
splits <- list(head = MY[junior == 0], jun = MY[junior == 1], urb = MY[urban == 1], rur = MY[urban == 0],
               elo = MY[edu_hi == 0], ehi = MY[edu_hi == 1], one = MY[multi_u6 == 0], two = MY[multi_u6 == 1])
H     <- lapply(splits, het)
H_emp <- lapply(splits, het, y = "employment")
jun_estimable <- isTRUE(H$jun$ok) && !is.na(H$jun$est)

# Who is the grandparent: age (health proxy), employment, sex
m_age  <- lapply(c(cc = "care_child", emp = "employment"), function(y) f(y, "gm_young + gm_old"))
m_work <- lapply(c(cc = "care_child", emp = "employment"), function(y) f(y, "gm_nowork + gm_work"))
m_sex  <- lapply(c(cc = "care_child", emp = "employment"), function(y) f(y, "gm_only + gf_only + gp_both"))
A <- list(
  young = lapply(m_age, coef_of, "gm_young"), old = lapply(m_age, coef_of, "gm_old"),
  dage = lapply(m_age, dcoef, "gm_young", "gm_old"),
  nowork = lapply(m_work, coef_of, "gm_nowork"), work = lapply(m_work, coef_of, "gm_work"),
  dwork = lapply(m_work, dcoef, "gm_nowork", "gm_work"),
  gmo = lapply(m_sex, coef_of, "gm_only"), gfo = lapply(m_sex, coef_of, "gf_only"),
  both = lapply(m_sex, coef_of, "gp_both"), dsex = lapply(m_sex, dcoef, "gm_only", "gf_only"))

# ---- Placebo: youngest own child aged 6-14, no child under six ------------------------
pl_outs <- c("care_child", "care_child_active", "care_child_passive", "unpaid_domestic", "employment")
PL <- lapply(setNames(pl_outs, pl_outs), function(y) list(
  u6 = coef_of(m_gm[[y]], "gm_any"),
  pl = coef_of(f(y, d = MP), "gm_any"),
  dd = NULL))
for (y in pl_outs) PL[[y]]$dd <- ddiff(PL[[y]]$u6, PL[[y]]$pl)
k_pl <- PL$care_child$pl; k_dd <- PL$care_child$dd; k_pl_emp <- PL$employment$pl

# ---- The older generation's own trade-offs ---------------------------------------------
# Members aged 45-80 in the generation above a married woman of childbearing age:
# head/spouse living with a married child's couple, or parent/in-law of the head living
# with a head-level couple. Treatment: a child under six in the household.
OG <- pd[age >= 45 & age <= 80 & !is.na(hh_n_under6) &
           ((rel %in% HEADLVL & n_junior_mw > 0) | (rel == PARENT & n_head_mw > 0))]
OG[, `:=`(young_gc = as.integer(hh_n_under6 > 0),
          special = as.integer(special_care %in% CODE$yes_no["yes"]))]
CVo <- c("i(age_band)", "i(edu_tier)", "urban", "i(mpce_quintile)", "married", "hh_n_6_14",
         "i(social_group_f)", "i(religion_f)", "special", "proxy_report")
fo <- function(y, d, x = "young_gc") reg(as.formula(paste(y, "~", x, "+", ctrl(d, CVo), fe(d))), d)
og_outs <- c("care_child", "care_child_active", "care_child_passive", "unpaid_domestic",
             "employment", "employed", "free_time", "sleep")
OGW <- OG[female == 1]; OGM <- OG[female == 0]
T_gm <- lapply(setNames(og_outs, og_outs), function(y) coef_of(fo(y, OGW), "young_gc"))
T_gf <- lapply(setNames(og_outs, og_outs), function(y) coef_of(fo(y, OGM), "young_gc"))
T_dd <- lapply(setNames(og_outs, og_outs), function(y) ddiff(T_gm[[y]], T_gf[[y]]))
n_ogw <- nrow(OGW); n_ogm <- nrow(OGM)
t_cc <- T_gm$care_child; t_emp <- T_gm$employment; t_ft <- T_gm$free_time; t_dom <- T_gm$unpaid_domestic
t_lfp <- T_gm$employed; t_sleep <- T_gm$sleep; tf_cc <- T_gf$care_child; td_cc <- T_dd$care_child
tf_emp <- T_gf$employment

# ---- Robustness -------------------------------------------------------------------------
MY[lk[o_age >= 45 | o_rel == PARENT, .(gm45 = as.integer(any(o_female == 1))), by = pid], on = "pid", gm45 := i.gm45]
MY[is.na(gm45), gm45 := 0L]
m1 <- m_gm$care_child
ob <- NA_real_; obe <- NA_real_
if (!is.null(m1)) {
  m0 <- reg(care_child ~ gm_any, MY[obs(m1)])
  ob <- tryCatch(oster_beta(m0, m1, "gm_any"), error = function(e) NA_real_)
}
if (!is.null(m_gm$employment)) {
  m0e <- reg(employment ~ gm_any, MY[obs(m_gm$employment)])
  obe <- tryCatch(oster_beta(m0e, m_gm$employment, "gm_any"), error = function(e) NA_real_)
}
cofn <- function(m, t) { k <- coef_of(m, t); k$n <- if (is.null(m)) NA_integer_ else nobs(m); k }
unw <- tryCatch(cofn(feols(as.formula(paste("care_child ~ gm_any +", ctrl(MY, CV), fe(MY))),
                              MY, cluster = ~fsu), "gm_any"), error = function(e) list(est = NA, se = NA, p = NA, n = NA))
RB <- list(
  "Baseline" = c(k_cc, n = nobs(m_gm$care_child)),
  "Only married woman aged 18--49 in the household" = cofn(f("care_child", d = MY[sole == 1]), "gm_any"),
  "Head-level mothers only (head or spouse of head)" = cofn(f("care_child", d = MY[junior == 0]), "gm_any"),
  "Mothers with a linked husband only" = cofn(f("care_child", d = MY[husband == 1]), "gm_any"),
  "Self-reported diaries only" = cofn(f("care_child", d = MY[proxy_report == 0]), "gm_any"),
  "Controlling for other women aged 15+" = cofn(f("care_child", extra = "n_other_women"), "gm_any"),
  "Controlling for household size" = cofn(f("care_child", extra = "hh_size"), "gm_any"),
  "Controlling for mother's generation (junior)" = cofn(f("care_child", extra = "junior"), "gm_any"),
  "Unweighted" = unw,
  "Any grandparent instead of grandmother" = cofn(f("care_child", "gp_any"), "gp_any"),
  "Grandmother defined as a woman aged 45 or above" = cofn(f("care_child", "gm45"), "gm45"))
k_any_cc <- cofn(f("any_cc"), "gm_any")
rb_est <- vapply(RB, function(k) as.numeric(k$est), numeric(1))
rb_sign_stable <- all(!is.na(rb_est)) && (all(rb_est < 0) || all(rb_est > 0))
rb_range <- range(rb_est, na.rm = TRUE)

# ---- Verdicts (drive every results-dependent sentence) ----------------------------------
sub_child <- is_neg(k_cc)
cc_up     <- is_pos(k_cc)
emp_up    <- is_pos(k_emp)
emp_down  <- is_neg(k_emp)
lfp_up    <- is_pos(k_lfp)
dom_up    <- is_pos(k_dom)
dom_down  <- is_neg(k_dom)
ft_up     <- is_pos(k_ft)
hh_more   <- is_pos(k_all)
hh_less   <- is_neg(k_all)
pas_only  <- is_neg(k_pas) && !is_neg(k_act)
act_too   <- is_neg(k_act)
pl_null   <- !is_sig(k_pl)
# Significant changes in grandmothers' other activities with a young grandchild
og_names <- c(unpaid_domestic = "domestic work", employment = "paid work", free_time = "free time", sleep = "sleep")
og_neg <- unname(og_names[vapply(names(og_names), function(y) is_neg(T_gm[[y]]), logical(1))])
og_pos <- unname(og_names[vapply(names(og_names), function(y) is_pos(T_gm[[y]]), logical(1))])
and_list <- function(x) if (length(x) <= 1) paste(x, collapse = "") else paste(paste(x[-length(x)], collapse = ", "), "and", x[length(x)])
gm_cost_cc  <- is_pos(t_cc)
gm_cost_emp <- is_neg(t_emp) || is_neg(t_lfp)
gm_cost_ft  <- is_neg(t_ft)
gf_cc_up    <- is_pos(tf_cc)
gf_less     <- is_pos(td_cc)
age_grad    <- is_sig(A$dage$cc)
work_grad   <- is_sig(A$dwork$cc)
sex_grad    <- is_sig(A$dsex$cc)
oster_same_sign <- !is.na(ob) && !is.na(k_cc$est) && sign(ob) == sign(k_cc$est)

# ---- Additional derived quantities ---------------------------
ci_incl0 <- function(k) isTRUE(!is.na(k$est) && (k$est - 1.96 * k$se) <= 0 && (k$est + 1.96 * k$se) >= 0)
cilo <- function(k, d = 1) .fmt(k$est - 1.96 * k$se, d)
cihi <- function(k, d = 1) .fmt(k$est + 1.96 * k$se, d)
emp_sign_differs <- length(unique(sign(na.omit(c(A$gmo$emp$est, A$both$emp$est, A$gfo$emp$est))))) > 1
cap_pattern <- age_grad && isTRUE(A$dage$cc$est > 0) && work_grad && isTRUE(A$dwork$cc$est < 0)
hx <- function(k) if (isTRUE(k$ok) && !is.na(k$est)) est_se(k) else "not estimable"
base_cc <- wmean(MY[gm_any == 0]$care_child, MY[gm_any == 0]$weight)
# Cross-check of the roster count against the household-size variable in the household file
share_roster_hh <- tryCatch({
  u <- pd[!duplicated(hh_id)]
  if (all(c("hh_size", "hh_n_roster") %in% names(u))) mean(u$hh_size == u$hh_n_roster, na.rm = TRUE) else NA_real_
}, error = function(e) NA_real_)

# ---- Adjusted differences by provider (Table who), same specification as eq. (1) -------
who_adj <- list(
  care_child = k_cc, father_cc = coef_of(f("father_cc"), "gm_any"), father_cc_linked = k_fa,
  gm_care_child = coef_of(f("gm_care_child"), "gm_any"), gf_care_child = coef_of(f("gf_care_child"), "gm_any"),
  others_cc = coef_of(f("others_cc"), "gm_any"), hh_cc_all = k_all)
# Total childcare conditional only on the numbers of children (under six, 6-14) and state and day FE
k_all_kids <- coef_of(reg(as.formula(paste("hh_cc_all ~ gm_any + hh_n_under6 + hh_n_6_14", fe(MY))), MY), "gm_any")
fa_l0 <- est_mean(MY[husband == 1 & gm_any == 0], "father_cc"); fa_l1 <- est_mean(MY[husband == 1 & gm_any == 1], "father_cc")
hh_all0 <- est_mean(MY[gm_any == 0], "hh_cc_all"); hh_all1 <- est_mean(MY[gm_any == 1], "hh_cc_all")
# ---- Oster: delta that would make the coefficient zero (Rmax = 1.3 R) --------------------
od0 <- function(m0, m1, term = "gm_any", mult = 1.3) {
  if (is.null(m0) || is.null(m1)) return(NA_real_)
  b0 <- coef(m0)[term]; b1 <- coef(m1)[term]; r0 <- fixest::r2(m0, "r2"); r1 <- fixest::r2(m1, "r2")
  rmax <- min(1, mult * r1); unname(b1 * (r1 - r0) / ((b0 - b1) * (rmax - r1)))
}

             ((rel %in% HEADLVL & n_junior_mw > 0) | (rel == PARENT & n_head_mw > 0))]
OG40[, `:=`(young_gc = as.integer(hh_n_under6 > 0), special = as.integer(special_care %in% CODE$yes_no["yes"]))]
```

\begin{abstract}
Do coresident grandmothers relieve mothers of childcare, and what do they give up? Using diaries for every household member in India's Time Use Survey 2024, I compare `r fn(n_my)` married mothers of children under six, `r pctx(share_gm, 0)` of whom live with a grandmother, and study `r fn(n_ogw)` women and `r fn(n_ogm)` men aged 45 to 80 in the generation above young married women. Older women living with a child under six report `r f1(t_cc$est)` minutes more childcare a day`r iff(length(og_neg) > 0, paste0(" and less ", and_list(og_neg)), "")`. Mothers' primary childcare differs little in the pooled estimate but is lower, with intervals excluding zero, in `r nw(n_rb_neg)` of `r nw(n_rb_alt)` alternative specifications and higher in `r nw(n_rb_pos)`; their secondary childcare is `r f1(abs(k_sec$est))` minutes lower. Their employment rate is `r f1(100 * abs(k_lfp$est))` percentage points `r iff(k_lfp$est < 0, 'lower', 'higher')` overall but `r f1(100 * abs(EG$lfp_g$est))` points `r iff(EG$lfp_g$est > 0, 'higher', 'lower')` within the mother's household generation. These are conditional associations, and grandmother care is associated with a large time cost for older women.
\end{abstract}

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} grandparents $\cdot$ childcare $\cdot$ three-generation households $\cdot$ patrilocality $\cdot$ time use $\cdot$ India

\noindent\textbf{JEL Classification:} D13 $\cdot$ J13 $\cdot$ J22


# Introduction

Grandparents are a major source of care for young children in many societies, and caring for grandchildren is a large part of the daily life of many older women. In India the family is the main childcare institution. Public provision for children under six runs mainly through the *anganwadi* centers of the Integrated Child Development Services, which focus on supplementary nutrition, health and pre-school education rather than full-day care, and women's labor force participation has long been low by international standards and slow to rise with education and income [@fletcher2017women_doi; @klasen2015stagnation_doi; @chatterjee2018indian; @afridi2018married]. A common presumption, in policy discussion and in the family itself, is that coresident grandparents, above all grandmothers, absorb much of the care of young children and so free mothers to work, rest or invest in other children. The presumption has empirical support elsewhere: in the United States, Europe, China and Japan the availability of grandparents is associated with, and in several quasi-experimental designs causes, higher maternal employment [@compton2014family; @posadas2013grandparents; @arpino2014grandparental; @bratti2018grandparental; @maurerfazio2011childcare; @sasaki2002causal; @ogawa1996family].

The same arrangement has a second side that matters for the economics of aging and of the family. The time that grandmothers give to grandchildren is a transfer from a generation whose own work, rest and health also matter, in a country whose older population is growing [@unfpa2023ageing_fix; @iips2020lasi_fix]. There are also reasons to doubt that the evidence from other settings carries over. Residence after marriage is predominantly patrilocal, so the coresident grandmother is typically the mother-in-law, and the literature describes the young daughter-in-law as the junior member of a hierarchy in which her mobility and work outside the home are shaped by her husband's parents [@dyson1983kinship; @kandiyoti1988bargaining; @jayachandran2015roots; @anukriti2020curse]. Women in joint households in rural India are less likely to be employed than women in nuclear households [@dhanaraj2019family]. A three-generation household is also a larger household, with more meals to cook. Coresidence can therefore add to a mother's work as well as bring a potential substitute for her childcare. I call these the *substitution* and *constraint* channels.

Which dominates is hard to learn from existing data. Surveys of labor supply record whether a grandparent lives nearby and whether the mother works, but not what either does with the day. Surveys of grandparents record whether they look after grandchildren, but not the mother's time on the same day. The literature has therefore inferred substitution from labor-market outcomes, and the cost of care to grandmothers has rarely been measured outside high-income settings.

This paper uses India's Time Use Survey 2024 [@nso2025tus], which records a 24-hour diary, coded to the International Classification of Activities for Time-Use Statistics 2016 (ICATUS) [@un2016icatus], for every household member aged six and above. Diaries of mothers and of the grandparents who live with them are kept for the same day, and the household roster's relationship codes identify, for each married woman, the generation above her. The identification rules matter. For a woman who is a married child of the head, or the spouse of one, the generation above is the head and the head's spouse, which is the typical patrilocal arrangement. And in a household where a son and his wife live with his parents and a child under six is present, the head's wife is usually that child's grandmother, not its mother: I exclude such women from the mother sample (`r fn(n_u6_dropgm)` of `r fn(n_u6_pool)` married women aged 18 to 49 in households with a child under six) and study them as grandmothers.

The analysis has four aims. The first is to compare the time use of mothers of children under six with and without a coresident grandmother, across the whole day. The second is to ask whether three-generation households provide the same childcare more cheaply or more care in total. The third is to estimate how a young grandchild is associated with the time use of grandmothers and grandfathers, which shows the cost of care to those who give it. The fourth is to ask which grandmothers matter (by age and employment), how the association differs across household arrangements, and whether it vanishes where it should, among mothers whose youngest child is of school age.

Each estimate below is reported with its 95% confidence interval (CI); means are reported with their standard error (SE). `r iff(sub_child, paste0("A coresident grandmother is associated with ", diff_txt(k_cc), " primary childcare by the mother a day."), iff(cc_up, paste0("A coresident grandmother is associated with ", diff_txt(k_cc), " primary childcare by the mother a day, not less."), paste0("The pooled association between a coresident grandmother and the mother's primary childcare is small: ", est_se(k_cc), ".")))` The association with the mother's paid work, including travel, is `r est_se(k_emp)`, and her probability of being employed by usual status is `r diff_pp(k_lfp)`. The minute estimates are fragile. The childcare estimate ranges from `r f1(rb_range[1])` to `r f1(rb_range[2])` minutes across the specifications in the robustness table, and subgroup estimates differ in size`r iff(emp_sign_differs, " and, for paid work, in sign", "")`. The grandmother's side is much clearer: in households with a child under six, the grandmother or grandmothers together report `r est_m(gm_cc)` of childcare a day, `r pct(gm_share_cc, 0)` of the combined raw (unadjusted) childcare minutes of mother and grandmother, and where a child under six is present they report `r diff_txt(t_cc)` primary childcare than other older women. `r iff(length(og_neg) > 0, paste0("They also report less ", and_list(og_neg), "."), "")` Summed over all household members aged 15 and above, primary childcare is `r diff_txt(k_all, "higher", "lower")` in households with a grandmother.

The paper contributes to three literatures. For the economics of grandparental childcare, it replaces inference from employment with same-day time measures for both generations, and shows that the association with mothers' time appears to depend on the grandmother's age and employment and on the household arrangement. For research on population aging and older women, it measures directly the time that older women give to grandchildren in a patrilocal, middle-income setting and the other parts of their day from which it comes. For the study of family structure and women's work in South Asia, it documents relationship-based rules for assigning young children and grandparents in rosters that do not record parent identifiers. The estimates are conditional associations, not causal effects: living arrangements are chosen jointly with fertility, work and care, and the survey is a single cross-section.

# Background and conceptual framework

## Grandparental care and maternal employment

A large literature finds that the availability of grandparents raises mothers' labor supply. In the United States, @compton2014family show that married women who live close to their mothers or mothers-in-law have higher labor force participation, and @posadas2013grandparents find that grandparent-provided childcare raises mothers' participation. In Europe, @dimova2011downward show that downward time transfers, mainly grandchild care, raise maternal labor supply, @arpino2014grandparental find a positive effect of grandparental support in Italy, and @bratti2018grandparental exploit Italian pension reforms that raised retirement ages, and so reduced grandmothers' availability, and find lower participation among their daughters. On the grandmothers' side, @frimmel2022grandmothers show with Austrian administrative data that a first grandchild raises the probability that a grandmother leaves the labor market, and @igel2011grandchild show that welfare-state arrangements shape the form of grandparental care across Europe. The evidence from Asia is closer to the Indian setting because coresidence, not proximity, is the usual arrangement. @ogawa1996family and @sasaki2002causal find that coresidence with parents or parents-in-law raised Japanese married women's employment, and @maurerfazio2011childcare find a similar association in urban China. For the United States, @bansak2026coresident find that living in an intergenerational household is positively related to employment among Asian women and negatively among white women.

Two features of this literature motivate the present paper. Almost all of it measures the consequence of grandparental care (maternal employment) rather than the care itself, and it comes mainly from settings in which coresidence or proximity is not tied to a strong patrilocal hierarchy. Where the grandmother is the mother-in-law and the head of the household, her presence may bring authority over the daughter-in-law's time as well as help with it.

## Older women's time, aging and intergenerational transfers

Grandparental childcare is a transfer of time between generations. Economic models distinguish altruistic from exchange motives for transfers [@cox1987motives; @altonji1997parental], and @cardia2003intergenerational show that grandparents' time is an important input into childcare. @albertini2007intergenerational document that European regimes differ in the frequency and intensity of time and money transfers across generations. Time transfers have an opportunity cost for the giver: @rupert2018grandchildren find that the arrival of grandchildren lowers grandmothers' labor supply in the United States, and @lumsdaine2015retirement that a new grandchild raises the probability that women retire. The evolutionary literature on grandmothering makes the same point from another angle, treating grandmothers' investment in grandchildren as a central and costly part of human life histories [@hawkes1998grandmothering; @sear2008keeps]. Time diaries for the older generation allow this cost to be measured directly, alongside the benefit to the mother, and allow it to be related to the grandmother's age and employment, which proxy her capacity to give care.

## Patrilocality and women's work in India

India differs from the settings above in ways that could reverse the sign of the association between coresidence and mothers' work. @dyson1983kinship argued that the kinship system of northern India, with village exogamy and patrilocal residence, limits women's autonomy, and @kandiyoti1988bargaining describes a patriarchal bargain in which young brides accept subordination in their husband's household in exchange for later authority as mothers-in-law. @anukriti2020curse show that coresident mothers-in-law restrict daughters-in-law's mobility and social networks in rural Uttar Pradesh; status concerns can lead households to withdraw women from work outside the home [@eswaran2013status], and social norms are a barrier to women's employment more broadly [@jayachandran2021social; @field2021account_fix]. @dhanaraj2019family find that women in nuclear households in rural India are more likely to work than women in joint households, and @afridi2018married decompose the fall in rural married women's participation over two decades. These studies observe employment, autonomy or decision-making, not time.

## Measuring childcare in time diaries

Time-diary research shows that childcare is the most gendered of household tasks and that its measurement is sensitive to definitions [@sayer2004parents; @bianchi2006changing; @craig2011share_doi; @hook2006care]. Primary childcare understates the time parents are responsible for children, because supervision is often recorded as a secondary activity or not at all [@folbre2005measure; @folbre2006measuring; @kalenkoski2008quality; @craig2007contemporary]. I therefore report active and passive primary care separately, and childcare recorded as a secondary activity, because a grandmother may take over supervision while the mother keeps the care that requires her, or the reverse.

## Conceptual framework

A mother allocates her day among childcare, domestic work, paid work and leisure. A coresident grandmother changes three things. She can supply childcare, which lowers the care the mother must provide (the substitution channel); this effect should rise with the grandmother's capacity, which declines with age and ill health and falls when she works herself. She raises household size and so domestic workload, and may need care herself (a workload channel). And in a patrilocal household she may raise the cost to the household of the daughter-in-law working outside the home (a norms channel); I group the last two as the constraint channel. Four predictions follow. If substitution is present, mothers' childcare is lower with a grandmother, more so for passive minding than for active care. Whether released time reaches paid work depends on the constraint channel, and if it is strong, released time shows up in domestic work or leisure. The grandmother's own time should show the other side, with more childcare and less of something else when a young grandchild is present. And substitution should be larger with grandmothers who have more capacity (younger, not employed) and concentrated where the youngest child is under six. The framework does not model the choice of living arrangement, the main threat to interpretation discussed below.

# Data and methods

## The Time Use Survey 2024

The Time Use Survey (TUS) 2024 was conducted by the National Statistics Office, Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, between January and December 2024 [@nso2025tus]. It covers a nationally representative sample of households in rural and urban India, drawn in a stratified multi-stage design with First Stage Units (FSU), that is, villages and urban blocks, as primary sampling units. Every member aged six and above reports a 24-hour diary for the day before the interview, from 4 a.m. to 4 a.m., in time slots that can contain several activities. Each activity is coded to ICATUS 2016 and flagged as major or minor (secondary). I use every activity record: `r fn(V$n_rows)` records for `r fn(V$n_diarists)` diarists in `r fn(V$n_households)` households and `r fn(V$n_fsu)` FSUs. Minutes of major activities are summed to the person-day, and all but `r nw(V$n_diaries_not1440)` of the `r fn(V$n_diarists)` diaries sum to exactly 1,440 minutes. `r iff(V$n_third_gender > 0, paste0("I exclude ", nw(V$n_third_gender), " persons recorded as third gender from the analyses because the sample is too small for separate estimates; they remain in household composition. "), "")`Weights are the survey multipliers, and standard errors are clustered on the FSU [@abadie2023cluster_doi; @solon2015weighting]. The survey construction checks and the sample construction are in Online Resource 1.

## Identifying mothers, children and grandparents

Children under six do not keep diaries but are listed on the household roster, so the number of under-six members is a direct count of roster members aged under six (the file contains members of all ages). `r iff(!is.na(share_roster_hh), paste0("As a check, the roster count of household members equals the household size recorded in the household file for ", pct(share_roster_hh, 1), " of households. "), "")`The roster does not record the identifier of each child's mother. The candidate mothers are married women aged 18 to 49 whose relationship to the head is head or spouse of head (head level), or married child or spouse of a married child (junior level). Women with other relationships, such as a brother's wife, are excluded because the roster does not identify the generation above them. In a household in which a married child of the head lives with a spouse, a child under six is far more likely to be the junior couple's child, that is, the head's grandchild, than a late-born child of the head. I therefore exclude from the mother sample head-level women who live with a junior-level married woman aged 15 to 49 (`r fn(n_u6_dropgm)` women), and study them as grandmothers. The analysis sample consists of the `r fn(n_my)` remaining women in households with at least one child under six. Of these, `r pct(share_jun, 0)` (weighted) are at junior level, and among junior-level mothers `r pct(share_dil, 0)` are daughters-in-law of the head. The husband is linked to `r pct(share_hus, 0)` of mothers through the roster; I keep mothers whose husbands live elsewhere in the sample, with an explicit indicator. A mother's own children aged six to 17, a control below, are also assigned by roster position: for a head-level mother they are the head's children of that age, and for a junior-level mother the head's grandchildren of that age, but only where the household contains a single child-in-law of the head. Otherwise the count is set to missing and replaced by zero with an indicator for an unknown count; the youngest own child used for the placebo sample follows the same rule.

For a head-level mother, the generation above her consists of members coded as father, mother, father-in-law or mother-in-law of the head. For a junior-level mother it consists of the head and the head's spouse aged 40 or above; the lower limit admits young grandmothers while excluding heads' spouses who are likely to be the mother's sisters-in-law rather than her parents-in-law. A coresident grandmother is at least one woman in this generation, and a coresident grandfather at least one man. Because each mother is matched to the specific members of the generation above her, a grandmother is never the mother herself (`r nw(n_self_links)` self-links). By this definition `r pct(share_gm, 0)` (weighted) of mothers of children under six live with a grandmother and `r pct(share_gf, 0)` with a grandfather; `r pct(share_gfo, 1)` live with a grandfather but no grandmother. Among mothers with a coresident grandmother, `r pct(share_jun_gm, 0)` are at junior level, so most three-generation households are of the patrilocal type in which the young family lives in the older generation's household. The median age of the youngest coresident grandmother is `r f0(gm_age_med)` years, `r pct(share_gm_young, 0)` of grandmothers are under 60, and `r pct(share_gm_work, 0)` report employment as their usual principal activity status (counts and weighted shares in Table \ref{tab:samplecons} of Online Resource 1).

## Time outcomes

Childcare is ICATUS 411 to 419 plus accompanying own children (442). Active care (411 to 415) covers physical care, medical care, teaching, talking and reading, and playing; passive care (416) is minding children. I also measure childcare recorded as a secondary activity, unpaid domestic services (division three) and within it food and meals (311 to 319), care of dependent adults (421 to 429 and 443), employment including related travel (division one), free time (divisions seven and eight) and sleep (911 to 919). Employment status is the usual principal activity status.



Table \ref{tab:desc} compares the raw time use of mothers with and without a coresident grandmother. Mothers without a grandmother report `r est_m(mo_cc0)` of primary childcare a day and mothers with one `r est_m(mo_cc1)`. The raw comparison mixes the grandmother's presence with everything that differs between joint and nuclear households, which motivates the regression approach.

```{r tab-desc}
dt <- rbind(means_table(MY, outs, "gp_lab", unname(out_lab[outs])),
            means_table(MY, "employed", "gp_lab", unname(out_lab["employed"]), digits = 3))
tab(dt, caption = paste0("Mothers of children under six: minutes per day by grandmother coresidence", syn_note()),
    label = "desc", align = c("l", "r", "r"), escape = FALSE,
    notes = "Married women aged 18--49 at head or junior level (head or spouse of head; married child of head or that child's spouse) in households with a child under six, excluding head-level women who live with a junior married woman of childbearing age. Survey-weighted means; FSU-clustered standard errors in parentheses. Employed is a share (three decimals). Primary childcare also includes other childcare (ICATUS 417--419) and accompanying children (442), not shown separately, so active and passive care do not sum to it.")
```

## Empirical strategy

For mother $i$ in household $h$, state $s$ and diary day $d$, I estimate

\begin{equation}\label{eq:main} y_{ihsd} = \beta\, \textit{GM}_{h} + X_{ih}'\gamma + \mu_s + \tau_d + \varepsilon_{ihsd}, \end{equation}

where $y_{ihsd}$ is a time outcome in minutes per day (or employment status) and $\textit{GM}_h$ indicates a coresident grandmother. $X_{ih}$ includes the mother's age band and education, the husband's education and usual employment (with a separate category for mothers without a linked husband), the household's per-capita consumption quintile, urban residence, the number of children under six and aged six to 14, the number of the mother's own children aged six to 17, caste group, religion, whether any member needs special care, and whether the diary was reported by a proxy. State fixed effects absorb regional kinship systems and labor markets, and day-of-week fixed effects absorb the weekly cycle. I do not control for household size in the main specification, because a grandmother raises it mechanically and the workload that comes with a larger household is part of the constraint channel; a robustness check adds it. I report 95% confidence intervals (CI) based on the normal approximation, not significance tests. In the text, an interval attached to a difference refers to the signed coefficient, with households without a grandmother as the reference.

The main threat to interpretation is selection into coresidence. Three-generation households differ from nuclear ones in wealth, caste, region and norms, and coresidence can respond to care needs: a grandmother may move in because a grandchild is born, or because she needs care herself. I read $\beta$ as a conditional association and assess it in four ways. First, I compare arrangements selected for different reasons. Junior-level mothers live in the older generation's household, the default patrilocal arrangement; head-level mothers whose parents or in-laws live with them have taken the older generation in, which may more often reflect the grandparents' need for support. Most junior-level mothers live with a grandmother (`r fn(n_jun_nogm)` do not, against `r fn(n_jun_gm)` who do), so the grandmother indicator is closely tied to the household arrangement, and where either cell has fewer than `r MIN_CELL` mothers I do not report the estimate. Second, I examine gradients that the substitution channel predicts but selection on fixed household traits does not obviously predict, by the grandmother's age, employment and sex. Third, I estimate the specification for mothers whose youngest child is aged six to 14 and who have no child under six in the household, among whom substitution of childcare should be weaker. Fourth, I report the bias-adjusted coefficient of @oster2019unobservable [see also @altonji2005selection].

The older generation's time is estimated on a separate sample of `r fn(n_ogw)` women and `r fn(n_ogm)` men aged 45 to 80 in the generation above a married woman of childbearing age. I regress the same outcomes on an indicator for a child under six in the household, with controls for age band, education, marital status, urban residence, consumption quintile, children aged six to 14, caste, religion, special care needs and proxy reporting, and state and day fixed effects. The comparison is between older-generation members whose grandchildren are young and those whose grandchildren are older or not yet born. Because every member of this sample already lives with a married woman of childbearing age, the comparison turns mainly on the timing of the junior couple's fertility. Fertility timing and living arrangements can still be chosen together, for example when a couple stays in the parental household because a child is born, so these estimates are also conditional associations. The older-generation sample starts at 45, while the grandmother link for junior-level mothers starts at 40. Online Resource 1 (Table \ref{tab:ogage}) re-estimates the older women's equations from age 40, and the robustness table defines the grandmother as a woman aged 45 or above.

## Ethics, data availability and the use of artificial intelligence tools

The analysis uses anonymized unit-level data released by the National Statistics Office and involved no contact with respondents; no ethical review was required. The microdata are available from the Ministry's microdata portal subject to its terms of use; analysis code will be made available on acceptance. Artificial intelligence (AI) tools (Claude (Anthropic) and other AI assistants) were used to help write and check analysis code, to check references and to draft text. The author reviewed and verified all code, results, references and text and takes full responsibility for the content.

# Results

## Mothers' time



Table \ref{tab:main} reports the main estimates. A coresident grandmother is associated with `r diff_txt(k_cc)` primary childcare by the mother a day. Relative to the mean of mothers without a grandmother, `r f1(base_cc)` minutes, the point estimate is `r pct(abs(k_cc$est) / base_cc, 0)` of the baseline. `r iff(ci_incl0(k_cc), paste0("The interval includes zero: the data are compatible with a reduction of up to ", pct(abs(min(k_cc$est - 1.96 * k_cc$se, 0)) / base_cc, 0), " of the baseline and with no change."), "")` The split by type of care shows `r est_se(k_act)` for active care and `r est_se(k_pas)` for passive minding. `r iff(pas_only, "The difference is concentrated in passive minding, the form of care most easily shared, while mothers retain active care, as the first prediction of the framework implies.", iff(act_too, "Grandmothers' presence is associated with less active care by mothers as well, not only less minding, so the difference extends to tasks that require more of the carer.", iff(ci_incl0(k_act) && ci_incl0(k_pas), "The intervals for both components include zero, and passive minding, the component the first prediction expects to fall most, is almost unchanged, so that prediction is not borne out in primary care.", "")))` `r iff(is_neg(k_sec), paste0("Mothers with a coresident grandmother do record less childcare as a secondary activity (", est_se(k_sec), ")", iff(ci_incl0(k_pas), ", so supervision is lower only when it is recorded as a secondary activity, not as primary minding.", ", so the lower supervision is not confined to primary care.")), paste0("Childcare recorded as a secondary activity differs by ", est_se(k_sec), "."))`

```{r tab-main}
rows <- c(outs, "employed")
rt <- data.frame(Outcome = unname(out_lab[rows]),
                 Mean = sapply(rows, function(y) if (y == "employed") f3(wmean(MY[gm_any == 0][[y]], MY[gm_any == 0]$weight)) else f1(wmean(MY[gm_any == 0][[y]], MY[gm_any == 0]$weight))),
                 Coefficient = sapply(rows, function(y) cell(coef_of(m_gm[[y]], "gm_any"), if (y == "employed") 3 else 2)),
                 `95 percent CI` = sapply(rows, function(y) ci_cell(coef_of(m_gm[[y]], "gm_any"), if (y == "employed") 3 else 2)),
                 N = sapply(rows, function(y) if (is.null(m_gm[[y]])) "--" else fn(nobs(m_gm[[y]]))),
                 check.names = FALSE)
tab(rt, caption = paste0("Coresident grandmother and mothers' time use", syn_note()), label = "main",
    align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"), escape = FALSE,
    notes = "Each row is a separate regression of the outcome (minutes per day, or a 0/1 indicator for usual employment) on an indicator for a coresident grandmother and the full control set, with state and day-of-week fixed effects. Mean: outcome mean for mothers without a coresident grandmother. Survey-weighted; FSU-clustered standard errors; 95 percent confidence intervals use the normal approximation. Primary childcare also includes other childcare (ICATUS 417--419) and accompanying children (442), not shown separately.")
```

The remaining rows show where the mother's day goes. Unpaid domestic work differs by `r est_se(k_dom)``r iff(is_pos(k_food) && !is_pos(k_dom), paste0(", but time on food and meals, the largest domestic task and the one most directly raised by household size, is higher by ", est_se(k_food), ", an interval that excludes zero"), paste0(", of which food and meals ", est_se(k_food)))`. Care of dependent adults differs by `r est_se(k_adult)`. Employment including travel differs by `r est_se(k_emp)`, and the probability that the mother's usual status is employed is `r diff_pp(k_lfp)`. `r iff(emp_up || lfp_up, "Some of any time released reaches paid work.", iff(emp_down || is_neg(k_lfp), "Neither pooled measure shows more paid work with a grandmother present, and the pooled employment-rate estimate is negative; the next paragraph examines whether this reflects the composition of the sample.", "Neither measure shows more paid work with a grandmother present."))` Free time is `r diff_txt(k_ft, "higher", "lower")` and sleep `r diff_txt(k_sleep, "higher", "lower")`. `r iff(!ci_incl0(k_ft) && !ci_incl0(k_sleep) && max(abs(c(k_ft$est, k_sleep$est))) < 10, "Both intervals exclude zero, but the differences amount to a few minutes in a day of 1,440.", "These are small differences relative to the day.")`

The pooled paid-work estimates mix two household arrangements with different levels of employment. Junior-level mothers, most of whom live with a grandmother, are less often employed than head-level mothers, whichever household they live in (Table \ref{tab:samplecons} of Online Resource 1), so a pooled comparison partly contrasts the two generations. Estimated separately, a grandmother is associated with more paid work among head-level mothers (`r hx(H_emp$head)`) and among junior-level mothers (`r hx(H_emp$jun)`; subgroup analysis below). Adding an indicator for the mother's generation to the pooled model (robustness checks below, panel B) turns the employment-minutes estimate into `r est_se(EG$emp_g)` and the employment-rate estimate into `r diff_pp(EG$lfp_g)`; adding household size as well gives `r est_se(EG$emp_gh)` and `r diff_pp(EG$lfp_gh)`. The negative pooled estimates are therefore consistent with composition: grandmothers live mainly in junior-level households, where mothers' employment is low. The within-generation estimates also vary across other subgroups (subgroup analysis below), so they do not establish a positive association for all mothers. Generation is itself part of how a grandmother comes to be present, so neither the pooled nor the within-generation estimate is causal, and the within-generation estimates give no sign that grandmothers' presence goes with less paid work by mothers of the same generation.

`r iff(!emp_up && !lfp_up && !sub_child, "Taken together, the pooled estimates show small differences in mothers' time and an association with primary childcare whose interval includes zero, and paid work is higher only once the mother's generation is held constant. They do not show that grandmothers relieve mothers of care, and, as the robustness checks and subgroup results below show, they hide differences by grandmother and by household arrangement.", iff(sub_child && !emp_up && !lfp_up, "Taken together, the pattern is consistent with the second prediction when the constraint channel is strong: grandmothers' presence is associated with less childcare by mothers but not with more employment. The data do not identify the constraint itself.", iff(emp_up || lfp_up, "Taken together, the results suggest that coresident grandmothers relax the time constraint of mothers enough to raise their paid work.", "")))`

## Who provides childcare in three-generation households



Table \ref{tab:who} (and Fig. \ref{fig:fig-providers} in Online Resource 1) decompose the childcare provided by household members. In households with a grandmother, the grandmother or grandmothers in the household together provide `r est_m(gm_cc)` of childcare a day. They also report `r est_m(gm_dom)` of domestic work and `r est_m(gm_empm)` of employment (lower panel of Table \ref{tab:who}), which shows what else their day contains. Summed over all members aged 15 and above, raw childcare is `r f1(hh_all1$est)` minutes with a grandmother and `r f1(hh_all0$est)` without, a gap of `r f1(round(hh_all1$est, 1) - round(hh_all0$est, 1))` minutes. Part of this gap reflects the larger number of children in three-generation households: conditional only on the numbers of children under six and aged six to 14 and on state and day fixed effects, the gap is `r est_se(k_all_kids)`, and with the full control set it is `r est_se(k_all)`. `r iff(hh_more, "Recorded adult childcare time is thus higher in three-generation households. Part of the difference may reflect two adults recording care of the same child at the same time, and part the care of several grandchildren at once; the diary does not identify the recipient.", iff(hh_less, "Children in three-generation households receive less adult childcare time in total, which would be the case if coresidence brings competing demands on the adults.", "The interval for total adult childcare includes zero."))` Among mothers with a linked husband, husbands' childcare averages `r f1(fa_l1$est)` minutes with a grandmother and `r f1(fa_l0$est)` without, and the adjusted difference is `r est_se(k_fa)`. `r iff(is_neg(k_fa), "A coresident grandmother is therefore associated with less care by fathers as well as with more care in the household as a whole.", "")`

```{r tab-who}
who_y <- c("care_child", "father_cc", "gm_care_child", "gf_care_child", "others_cc", "hh_cc_all")
who_l <- c("Mother", "Husband", "Grandmother(s)", "Grandfather(s)",
           "Other members aged 15+", "All members aged 15+")
mcell <- function(r) paste0(.fmt(r$est, 1), " (", .fmt(r$se, 1), ")")
mrow <- function(y, d = MY) c(mcell(est_mean(d[gm_any == 0], y)), mcell(est_mean(d[gm_any == 1], y)))
wt <- rbind(
  c("Mother", mrow("care_child"), cse(who_adj$care_child)),
  c("Husband (zero if not linked)", mrow("father_cc"), cse(who_adj$father_cc)),
  c("\\quad Linked husbands only", mrow("father_cc", MY[husband == 1]), cse(who_adj$father_cc_linked)),
  c("Grandmother(s), together", "0.0", mcell(gm_cc), cse(who_adj$gm_care_child)),
  c("Grandfather(s), together", mrow("gf_care_child"), cse(who_adj$gf_care_child)),
  c("Other members aged 15+", mrow("others_cc"), cse(who_adj$others_cc)),
  c("All members aged 15+", mrow("hh_cc_all"), cse(who_adj$hh_cc_all)),
  c("\\quad conditional on numbers of children only", "", "", cse(k_all_kids)),
  c("\\textit{Grandmother(s), other activities}", "", "", ""),
  c("\\quad Unpaid domestic work", "--", mcell(gm_dom), ""),
  c("\\quad Employment (incl. travel)", "--", mcell(gm_empm), ""))
wt <- as.data.frame(wt, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
names(wt) <- c("Provider", "No grandmother", "Grandmother present", "Adjusted difference [95\\% CI]")
tab(wt, caption = paste0("Childcare minutes per day by provider, households with a child under six", syn_note()),
    label = "who", align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"), escape = FALSE,
    notes = paste0("Unit: mothers in the analysis sample (", fn(n_my), "). Columns 1--2: minutes of primary childcare of each household member, survey-weighted means with FSU-clustered standard errors in parentheses. Column 3: coefficient on the grandmother indicator [95 percent confidence interval] from the main specification, with that row as the outcome; the linked-husband row is estimated on mothers with a linked husband (", fn(MY[husband == 1, .N]), "). Husbands who are not linked through the roster count as zero in the husband row and their care falls in Other members. The conditional row controls only for the numbers of children under six and aged 6--14 and state and day fixed effects. All members is the household total and includes care given to other children in the household; its raw difference is ", f1(round(hh_all1$est, 1) - round(hh_all0$est, 1)), " minutes. Lower panel: minutes of the grandmother(s) in households with a grandmother."))
```

## The older generation's time



Table \ref{tab:og} (and Fig. \ref{fig:fig-og} in Online Resource 1) turns to the providers of care. The older-generation sample can include a woman aged 45 to 49 who is herself the mother of a late-born child; dropping the `r fn(n_og4549)` women aged 45 to 49 leaves `r fn(n_ogw50)` women and gives a childcare association of `r est_se(T50$care_child)` (Table \ref{tab:ogage} in Online Resource 1), close to the main estimate. Among older-generation women, a child under six in the household is associated with `r diff_txt(t_cc)` primary childcare a day, against a mean of `r f1(wmean(OGW[young_gc == 0]$care_child, OGW[young_gc == 0]$weight))` minutes for women without a young grandchild. `r iff(gm_cost_cc, "On the care side the third prediction of the framework holds: grandmothers report more childcare when a young grandchild is present.", "Grandmothers do not report more childcare when a young grandchild is present, which casts doubt on the substitution channel itself.")` The associations with grandmothers' domestic work (`r est_se(t_dom)`), paid work (`r est_se(t_emp)`), employment status (`r diff_pp(t_lfp)`), free time (`r est_se(t_ft)`) and sleep (`r est_se(t_sleep)`) show what else differs in their day. `r iff(length(og_neg) > 0, paste0("Grandmothers with a young grandchild report less ", and_list(og_neg), ", with confidence intervals that exclude zero. ", iff("domestic work" %in% og_neg && is_pos(k_food), "Mothers' total domestic work does not differ with a grandmother present (Table \\ref{tab:main}), and across its components (Table \\ref{tab:domparts} in Online Resource 1) higher time on food and meals is offset by lower time on cleaning, so these estimates, which come from separate samples and treatments, give no clear sign of domestic tasks moving from the grandmother to the mother; the placebo for domestic work (below) also suggests a larger household workload for mothers. ", ""), iff(length(og_cost) > 0, paste0("The extra care they report is accompanied by less ", and_list(og_cost), ". "), ""), iff(any(grepl("free time", og_neg)) && abs(t_ft$est) == max(abs(c(t_dom$est, t_ft$est, t_sleep$est))), paste0("The fall in free time is the largest, at ", pct(abs(t_ft$est) / wmean(OGW[young_gc == 0]$free_time, OGW[young_gc == 0]$weight), 0), " of the mean for women without a young grandchild."), "")), "No component is clearly lower, so the diaries do not reveal a single activity from which the extra childcare is drawn.")` `r iff(is_neg(t_emp) || is_neg(t_lfp), "Their paid work is also lower, as in the evidence for the United States [@rupert2018grandchildren].", paste0("Their paid work does not fall", iff(length(og_neg) > 0, paste0(", so in this sample the extra childcare is accompanied by less ", and_list(og_cost), " but not by less paid work"), ""), "."))`

```{r tab-og}
og_lab <- c(care_child = "Childcare (primary)", care_child_active = "\\quad Active childcare",
            care_child_passive = "\\quad Passive childcare (minding)", unpaid_domestic = "Unpaid domestic work",
            employment = "Employment (incl. travel)", employed = "Employed (usual status, share)",
            free_time = "Free time", sleep = "Sleep")
ot <- data.frame(Outcome = unname(og_lab[og_outs]),
                 `Mean, women` = sapply(og_outs, function(y) (if (y == "employed") f3 else f1)(wmean(OGW[young_gc == 0][[y]], OGW[young_gc == 0]$weight))),
                 `Older women` = sapply(og_outs, function(y) cse(T_gm[[y]], if (y == "employed") 3 else 2)),
                 `Older men` = sapply(og_outs, function(y) cse(T_gf[[y]], if (y == "employed") 3 else 2)),
                 Difference = sapply(og_outs, function(y) cse(T_dd[[y]], if (y == "employed") 3 else 2)),
                 check.names = FALSE)
tab(ot, caption = paste0("The older generation: time use and a child under six in the household", syn_note()),
    label = "og", align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"), escape = FALSE,
    notes = paste0("Members aged 45--80 in the generation above a married woman of childbearing age (", fn(n_ogw), " women, ", fn(n_ogm), " men). Estimate [95 percent confidence interval] for an indicator for a child under six in the household, separately for women and men; Difference: women minus men, with a standard error that ignores the covariance of the two estimates (conservative, since grandmothers and grandfathers often share a household). Mean: women without a child under six. Controls: age band, education, marital status, urban, consumption quintile, children 6--14, caste, religion, special care need, proxy report; state and day fixed effects. FSU-clustered standard errors; 95 percent confidence intervals use the normal approximation."))
```
