For older-generation men, the corresponding childcare association is `r est_se(tf_cc)`, and the women-minus-men difference is `r est_se(td_cc)`. `r iff(gf_less, "The care response of the older generation falls overwhelmingly on grandmothers, mirroring the gender division of care in the middle generation.", iff(is_sig(td_cc), "Grandfathers' childcare responds more than grandmothers' on this measure.", "The interval for the difference between grandmothers and grandfathers includes zero."))` Paid work of older men differs by `r est_se(tf_emp)`.`r iff(is_pos(tf_emp) && !is_pos(t_emp), paste0(" It is higher for older men and not clearly for older women, but the women-minus-men difference, ", est_se(T_dd$employment), ", ", iff(ci_incl0(T_dd$employment), "is imprecise and includes zero, so the data do not establish a gender difference in the paid-work response.", "excludes zero.")), "")`

## Which grandmothers matter



Table \ref{tab:gptype} examines the fourth prediction. Grandmother age proxies for health and stamina, which the survey does not measure directly. Relative to mothers without a grandmother, the coefficient on mothers' childcare is `r est_se(A$young$cc)` for a grandmother under 60 and `r est_se(A$old$cc)` for a grandmother aged 60 or older; the difference is `r est_se(A$dage$cc)`. `r iff(age_grad && isTRUE(A$dage$cc$est < 0), "Younger grandmothers are associated with a larger reduction in mothers' childcare, as the capacity part of the substitution channel predicts.", iff(age_grad, "The reduction in mothers' childcare is concentrated where the grandmother is 60 or older, and the interval for the difference excludes zero. This runs against a simple capacity story in which younger grandmothers are fitter, but it is consistent with older grandmothers being less likely to be in paid work and so more available at home.", "The interval for the difference by grandmother age includes zero."))`

```{r tab-who-gp}
gr <- data.frame(
  Comparison = c("Grandmother under 60", "Grandmother 60 or older", "\\quad Difference (under 60 minus 60+)",
                 "Grandmother not employed", "Grandmother employed", "\\quad Difference (not employed minus employed)",
                 "Grandmother only", "Grandfather only", "Both grandparents",
                 "\\quad Difference (grandmother only minus grandfather only)"),
  Childcare = c(cse(A$young$cc), cse(A$old$cc), cse(A$dage$cc), cse(A$nowork$cc), cse(A$work$cc), cse(A$dwork$cc),
                cse(A$gmo$cc), cse(A$gfo$cc), cse(A$both$cc), cse(A$dsex$cc)),
  Employment = c(cse(A$young$emp), cse(A$old$emp), cse(A$dage$emp), cse(A$nowork$emp), cse(A$work$emp), cse(A$dwork$emp),
                 cse(A$gmo$emp), cse(A$gfo$emp), cse(A$both$emp), cse(A$dsex$emp)),
  check.names = FALSE)
tab(gr, caption = paste0("Mothers' childcare and employment minutes by type of coresident grandparent", syn_note()),
    label = "gptype", align = c("l", "r", "r"), escape = FALSE,
    notes = "Each block is one regression per outcome with mutually exclusive indicators; the omitted group is mothers with no coresident grandmother (first two blocks) or no coresident grandparent (third block). Age is that of the youngest coresident grandmother; employment is usual principal activity status. Controls as in the main specification. Estimate [95 percent confidence interval]; FSU-clustered.")
```

An employed grandmother has less time to give. The coefficient is `r est_se(A$nowork$cc)` for a grandmother who is not employed and `r est_se(A$work$cc)` for one who is, a difference of `r est_se(A$dwork$cc)`. `r iff(work_grad && isTRUE(A$dwork$cc$est < 0), paste0("The lower childcare is concentrated among mothers whose grandmother is not in paid work; with an employed grandmother mothers' childcare is ", iff(is_pos(A$work$cc), "higher", "not lower"), "."), iff(work_grad, "Contrary to the capacity prediction, the association is stronger with employed grandmothers.", "The interval for the difference by grandmother's employment includes zero."))` Grandmothers' age, employment and household position are related, and employment is itself a choice made jointly with the care they provide, so these comparisons are descriptive.

The last block separates grandmothers from grandfathers. The coefficient on mothers' childcare is `r est_se(A$gmo$cc)` for a grandmother without a grandfather, `r est_se(A$gfo$cc)` for a grandfather without a grandmother, and `r est_se(A$both$cc)` for both together. `r iff(ci_incl0(A$both$cc) && is_neg(A$gmo$cc), "With both grandparents present mothers' childcare is not lower, so the pooled reduction comes from households with a single coresident grandparent. ", "")``r iff(sex_grad && isTRUE(A$dsex$cc$est < 0), "The association is more negative for grandmothers than for grandfathers, with an interval for the difference that excludes zero.", iff(sex_grad, "The association is more negative for grandfathers, which runs against the gendered-norm prediction.", paste0("The interval for the difference between grandmothers and grandfathers includes zero; households with only a grandfather are a small share of the sample (", pct(share_gfo, 1), "), so this comparison is imprecise.")))` Mothers' paid work is `r diff_txt(A$gmo$emp, "higher", "lower")` with a grandmother only and `r diff_txt(A$both$emp, "higher", "lower")` with both grandparents`r iff(emp_sign_differs, ", so the pooled employment estimate averages associations of different sign", "")`. `r iff(age_grad || work_grad || sex_grad, "These gradients do not follow the capacity ordering of the framework uniformly: some fit substitution where the older generation has time to give and others run against it, and grandmother age and employment are themselves tied to the household arrangement, so they do not separate substitution from selection.", "Because none of these gradients is distinguishable from zero, they do not help to separate substitution from selection.")`

## Differences by household arrangement



Table \ref{tab:het} reports the estimates by subsample. For head-level mothers, whose parents or in-laws live in their household, the childcare association is `r hx(H$head)` and the employment association `r hx(H_emp$head)`. `r iff(jun_estimable, paste0("For junior-level mothers, who live in their in-laws' or parents' household, the childcare association is ", hx(H$jun), " and the employment association ", hx(H_emp$jun), ", estimated from only ", fn(n_jun_nogm), " junior-level mothers without a grandmother. The two arrangements are selected for different reasons, the first possibly more often by the grandparents' need for support and the second by the patrilocal norm, and ", iff(is_sig(ddiff(H$head, H$jun)), "the estimates differ.", "the estimates are too imprecise to distinguish them.")), paste0("For junior-level mothers, who live in the older generation's household, the estimate is not reported: only ", fn(n_jun_nogm), " of the ", fn(n_jun_nogm + n_jun_gm), " junior-level mothers live without a coresident grandmother, too few to separate her presence from the arrangement itself."))` `r iff(!jun_estimable, "The head-level estimate therefore describes mothers whose parents or in-laws have joined their household, and it should not be generalized to the junior arrangement.", "")` Because most junior-level mothers live with a grandmother, the pooled grandmother indicator partly captures the difference between the two arrangements. With a control for the mother's generation the estimate is `r est_se(RB[[8]])` (see the robustness checks below), compared with `r est_se(k_cc)` in the pooled specification.

```{r tab-het}
hl <- c(head = "Head-level mother (grandparents live in her household)",
        jun = "Junior-level mother (lives in the older generation's household)",
        urb = "Urban", rur = "Rural", elo = "Mother below secondary education",
        ehi = "Mother secondary education or above", one = "One child under six", two = "Two or more children under six")
hcell <- function(k) if (!isTRUE(k$ok)) "not estimable" else cse(k)
ht <- data.frame(Subsample = unname(hl[names(splits)]),
                 Childcare = sapply(names(splits), function(s) hcell(H[[s]])),
                 Employment = sapply(names(splits), function(s) hcell(H_emp[[s]])),
                 N = sapply(names(splits), function(s) fn(nrow(splits[[s]]))), check.names = FALSE)
tab(ht, caption = paste0("Heterogeneity: grandmother coresidence and mothers' childcare and employment minutes", syn_note()),
    label = "het", align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
    notes = paste0("Main specification, estimated separately by subsample. Estimate [95 percent confidence interval] for the grandmother indicator. Not estimable: fewer than ", MIN_CELL, " mothers with or without a coresident grandmother in the subsample.", iff(all(vapply(H, function(k) isTRUE(k$ok), logical(1))), " No subsample falls below it.", ""), " Intervals are not adjusted for multiple comparisons across subgroups; individual subgroup estimates should be read as exploratory."))
```

Across urban and rural households the childcare associations are `r hx(H$urb)` and `r hx(H$rur)`. By the mother's education they are `r hx(H$elo)` below secondary and `r hx(H$ehi)` at secondary or above. More educated mothers have better labor-market options, so if grandmothers' help reaches paid work anywhere it should be among them; the corresponding employment associations are `r hx(H_emp$elo)` and `r hx(H_emp$ehi)`, and by urban and rural residence `r hx(H_emp$urb)` and `r hx(H_emp$rur)`. With one child under six the childcare association is `r hx(H$one)`, and with two or more `r hx(H$two)`. `r iff(isTRUE(H_emp$urb$ok) && isTRUE(H_emp$rur$ok) && sign(H_emp$urb$est) != sign(H_emp$rur$est), "The employment associations differ in sign between urban and rural mothers, which again shows that the pooled employment estimate should not be read as evidence of no association.", "")`

## A placebo: mothers of school-age children



If grandmothers substitute for the care of young children, the association with mothers' childcare should be weaker where the youngest child is of school age and needs less supervision. If instead the main estimate reflects fixed differences between joint and nuclear households, it should be similar for both groups of mothers. Table \ref{tab:placebo} reports the comparison for `r fn(n_mp)` mothers whose youngest identified own child is aged six to 14 and who have no child under six in the household. The childcare association is `r est_se(k_pl)` in this group, against `r est_se(k_cc)` in the analysis sample, and the difference between the two is `r est_se(k_dd)`. `r iff(sub_child && pl_null && is_neg(k_dd), "The association with childcare is confined to mothers of young children, as substitution implies and fixed-trait selection does not.", iff(sub_child && !is_neg(k_dd), "The association is not weaker for mothers of school-age children, which leaves room for selection on household traits to explain part of the main estimate.", iff(!sub_child, "Because the main childcare estimate is itself small, the childcare comparison is not informative on its own.", "")))` The placebo is not fully clean. The association with domestic work, which the constraint channel predicts should not depend on the child's age, is `r est_se(PL$unpaid_domestic$pl)` in the placebo group and `r est_se(PL$unpaid_domestic$u6)` in the analysis sample`r iff(is_pos(PL$unpaid_domestic$pl), ", so a grandmother's presence is associated with more domestic work among mothers of school-age children, for whom the substitution channel should be weak. This pattern is consistent with a workload effect of larger households and with selection, and it means the placebo cannot rule out that part of the main estimates reflects household traits", "")`.

```{r tab-placebo}
plab <- c(care_child = "Childcare (primary)", care_child_active = "\\quad Active childcare",
          care_child_passive = "\\quad Passive childcare (minding)", unpaid_domestic = "Unpaid domestic work",
          employment = "Employment (incl. travel)")
pt <- data.frame(Outcome = unname(plab[pl_outs]),
                 `Child under six` = sapply(pl_outs, function(y) cse(PL[[y]]$u6)),
                 `Youngest child 6--14` = sapply(pl_outs, function(y) cse(PL[[y]]$pl)),
                 Difference = sapply(pl_outs, function(y) cse(PL[[y]]$dd)), check.names = FALSE)
tab(pt, caption = paste0("Placebo: grandmother coresidence for mothers whose youngest child is aged 6 to 14", syn_note()),
    label = "placebo", align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"), escape = FALSE,
    notes = paste0("Estimate [95 percent confidence interval] for the grandmother indicator. Column 1: analysis sample (", fn(n_my), " mothers). Column 2: mothers defined in the same way with no child under six in the household and an identified youngest own child aged 6 to 14 (", fn(n_mp), " mothers). Difference: column 1 minus column 2, with a standard error that ignores the covariance of the two estimates. Controls as in the main specification."))
```

## Robustness



Table \ref{tab:robust} collects robustness checks for the childcare estimate. Restricting to households with a single married woman aged 18 to 49, where the child under six is most likely hers, gives `r est_se(RB[[2]])`. Restricting to head-level mothers gives `r est_se(RB[[3]])`. Requiring a linked husband gives `r est_se(RB[[4]])`, and dropping proxy-reported diaries gives `r est_se(RB[[5]])`. Adding the number of other adult women gives `r est_se(RB[[6]])`; adding household size gives `r est_se(RB[[7]])`; and adding an indicator for the mother's generation gives `r est_se(RB[[8]])`. The unweighted estimate is `r est_se(RB[[9]])`, and broadening the treatment to any grandparent gives `r est_se(RB[[10]])`. On the extensive margin, a grandmother is associated with a `r diff_pp(k_any_cc)` probability that the mother reports any primary childcare. `r iff(rb_sign_stable, paste0("All estimates have the same sign, ranging from ", f1(rb_range[1]), " to ", f1(rb_range[2]), " minutes."), paste0("The estimates range from ", f1(rb_range[1]), " to ", f1(rb_range[2]), " minutes and do not all share a sign, so the main childcare estimate should be read as fragile: its sign and size depend on whether household size, the mother's generation or the household arrangement is held constant."))` Of the `r nw(n_rb_alt)` alternative childcare specifications, `r nw(n_rb_neg)` give a negative estimate whose interval excludes zero and `r nw(n_rb_pos)` a positive one, so the pooled baseline is closer to zero than most alternatives. The bias-adjusted coefficient of @oster2019unobservable, which assumes that unobservables are as important as observables and that the maximum attainable $R^2$ is 1.3 times that of the full model, is `r f2(ob)` for childcare and `r f2(obe)` for employment minutes. The degree of selection on unobservables, relative to observables, that would reduce the coefficient to zero is `r f2(od_cc)` for childcare and `r f2(od_emp)` for employment; `r iff(isTRUE(od_cc < 0) && isTRUE(od_emp < 0), paste0("both values are negative, so only selection on unobservables opposite in direction to selection on observables could reduce the coefficients to zero", iff(abs(od_emp) < 1, ", and for employment the required degree is below one in absolute value, so the employment estimate is not robust in this sense.", "."), " Because both baseline estimates are close to zero with intervals that include it, these delta values are of limited informativeness."), "")` Defining the grandmother as a woman aged 45 or above, the lower limit of the older-generation sample, gives `r est_se(RB[[11]])` for childcare and `r est_se(k45$emp)` for employment minutes. The stricter definition moves the childcare estimate towards the negative alternatives, so the near-zero baseline should not be read as evidence of no substitution; nor does the stricter definition change the conclusion on paid work, whose interval includes zero, as in the baseline. `r iff(oster_same_sign && sub_child, "The childcare estimate keeps its sign under this adjustment.", iff(sub_child, "Under this adjustment the childcare estimate changes sign, so a moderate degree of selection on unobservables could account for it.", ""))`

```{r robust}
nf <- function(k) if (is.null(k$n) || is.na(k$n)) "" else fn(k$n)
EB <- list("Baseline, employment minutes" = c(k_emp, n = n_emp_main),
           "Employment minutes, controlling for mother's generation" = EG$emp_g,
           "Employment minutes, controlling for generation and household size" = EG$emp_gh,
           "Employment minutes, grandmother aged 45 or above" = k45$emp,
           "Baseline, employed (usual status, share)" = c(k_lfp, n = n_lfp_main),
           "Employed (share), controlling for mother's generation" = EG$lfp_g,
           "Employed (share), controlling for generation and household size" = EG$lfp_gh)
eb_d <- c(2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3)
n_cc_main <- nobs(m_gm$care_child)
rb <- data.frame(Check = c("\\textit{A. Mothers' primary childcare (minutes)}", names(RB), "Extensive margin: any primary childcare (share)",
                           "Oster bias-adjusted, childcare (delta = 1, Rmax = 1.3 R)",
                           "Oster delta for a zero coefficient, childcare (Rmax = 1.3 R)",
                           "\\textit{B. Mothers' paid work}", names(EB),
                           "Oster bias-adjusted, employment minutes (delta = 1, Rmax = 1.3 R)",
                           "Oster delta for a zero coefficient, employment minutes (Rmax = 1.3 R)"),
                 Estimate = c("", vapply(RB, cell, character(1)), cell(k_any_cc, 3), f2(ob), f2(od_cc),
                              "", mapply(cell, EB, eb_d), f2(obe), f2(od_emp)),
                 `95 percent CI` = c("", vapply(RB, ci_cell, character(1)), ci_cell(k_any_cc, 3), "", "",
                                     "", mapply(ci_cell, EB, eb_d), "", ""),
                 N = c("", vapply(RB, nf, character(1)), nf(k_any_cc), fn(n_cc_main), fn(n_cc_main),
                       "", vapply(EB, nf, character(1)), fn(n_emp_main), fn(n_emp_main)),
                 check.names = FALSE)
tab(rb, caption = paste0("Robustness: mothers' primary childcare and paid work", syn_note()), label = "robust",
    align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"), escape = FALSE,
    notes = "Coefficient on the grandmother indicator (or any grandparent) in the main specification, unless stated. N is the number of mothers in each regression. The extensive-margin row is a linear probability model. The Oster rows use the short regression without controls or fixed effects on the same sample; the bias-adjusted estimate sets delta = 1, and the delta rows give the relative degree of selection on unobservables that would make the coefficient zero. The age-45 rows require the grandmother of a junior-level mother to be aged 45 or above instead of 40. The generation control is an indicator for a junior-level mother.")
```

# Discussion and conclusion

## Interpretation

`r iff(!sub_child && !(emp_up || lfp_up), paste0("The pooled association between a coresident grandmother and a mother's primary childcare is small, with a 95% CI of ", cilo(k_cc), " to ", cihi(k_cc), " minutes a day, and the interval for paid work, ", cilo(k_emp), " to ", cihi(k_emp), " minutes, also includes zero. These intervals describe one specification. The childcare estimate changes size and sign when the comparison changes (Table \\ref{tab:robust}), and it differs by grandmother and by household arrangement (Tables \\ref{tab:gptype} and \\ref{tab:het}). The pooled estimate is therefore best read as an average over different associations, not as evidence that grandmothers' care has no effect on mothers' time."), "")`

The clearest evidence concerns grandmothers. Where a child under six is present, grandmothers report much more childcare than other older women`r iff(length(og_neg) > 0, paste0(", and less ", and_list(og_neg)), "")``r iff(!is_neg(t_emp) && !is_neg(t_lfp), ", while their paid work does not fall", "")`. `r iff(length(og_cost) > 0, paste0("Grandmothering in this setting is associated with substantially more childcare time by older women, together with less ", and_list(og_cost), "."), "Grandmothering in this setting is associated with substantially more childcare time by older women.")` `r iff(gm_cost_cc && hh_more, "Recorded adult childcare in three-generation households is also higher in total, although part of this may reflect simultaneous or shared recording.", "")`

For mothers, three readings are consistent with the pattern, and the evidence allows only a partial ranking. The first is substitution where the grandmother has time. `r iff(cap_pattern, paste0("Mothers' childcare is lower where the grandmother is 60 or older, and in a separate split where she is not in paid work, and it is higher where she is under 60 (", est_se(A$young$cc), ") or employed (", est_se(A$work$cc), ")", iff(is_neg(H$head), "; among head-level mothers the reduction is larger", ""), ". The age and employment splits are separate regressions, not a joint classification, and with both grandparents present mothers' childcare is not lower."), "The gradients by the grandmother's age and employment (Table \\ref{tab:gptype}) are the evidence on this reading, and they are not uniformly in the predicted direction.")` The second is the constraint channel: a larger household and a senior woman's authority raise the mother's domestic load and the wedge on work outside the home, so any childcare time released is absorbed`r iff(is_pos(k_food), "; mothers' time on food and meals is higher, but their total domestic work is not, so the diaries give this reading little direct support", "")`. The third is selection: mothers who choose, or are placed in, three-generation households differ in ways that also shape their time. Gradients by the grandmother's characteristics are harder to attribute to fixed household traits, but selection remains open: the pooled estimate is sensitive to the specification`r iff(is_pos(PL$unpaid_domestic$pl), ", and the placebo for domestic work is not clean", "")`. `r iff(is_neg(k_fa), "Fathers' childcare is also lower with a grandmother present, among mothers with a linked husband as well as overall.", "")`

Studies in the United States, Europe, Japan and China find that grandparents are associated with, and in several quasi-experimental designs raise, maternal employment [@compton2014family; @dimova2011downward; @bratti2018grandparental; @sasaki2002causal; @maurerfazio2011childcare]. `r iff(!emp_up && !lfp_up, paste0("The pooled estimates here show no such association in India", iff(is_neg(k_lfp) && !ci_incl0(k_lfp), paste0(" (mothers' paid-work minutes differ little, and their employment rate is ", f1(100 * abs(k_lfp$est)), " percentage points lower)"), ""), ", even though grandmothers provide ", pct(gm_share_cc, 0), " of the combined raw (unadjusted) childcare minutes of the two women. Within the mother's household generation, however, the employment rate is ", diff_pp(EG$lfp_g), ", so the Indian estimates are not clearly at odds with those studies: one difference is that grandmothers here live mainly in junior-level households, where mothers' employment is low, although the within-generation estimate varies across subgroups and the Oster bounds for employment are weak. Whether household norms in such households restrict married women's work [@dhanaraj2019family; @anukriti2020curse; @jayachandran2021social] cannot be established with these data."), "The estimates here show a positive association with mothers' paid work, in line with the studies above.")` The Norwegian finding that formal childcare mainly crowded out informal care [@havnes2011money] is a useful parallel: when one form of care replaces another, the effect on mothers' work depends on what else constrains it.

## Implications for research and policy

Policy on childcare and policy on older people's wellbeing are usually considered separately. These results suggest that they interact. Family care appears costly to those who provide it: older women report less free time and sleep when a young grandchild is present. As India's population ages [@unfpa2023ageing_fix; @iips2020lasi_fix], the supply of grandmother care will depend on older women's health, employment and household position, and the implicit cost to them belongs in any assessment of how families, and public provision, share the care of young children. Expanding formal childcare may matter for mothers in extended households as well as in nuclear ones, although its effect will depend on whether the constraints of the extended household also bind on the use of formal care. All of these statements rest on conditional associations from one cross-section and should be treated with caution.

## Limitations

The limitations are those of a single cross-section of diaries. Living arrangements are chosen, and the gradients, the placebo, the comparison of arrangements and the coefficient-stability bounds are partly inconclusive and do not eliminate the scope for selection. Most junior-level mothers live with a grandmother, so the grandmother indicator is entangled with the household arrangement, and a design that compares mothers within the same arrangement would be preferable. The survey offers no credible instrument for coresidence. One diary day per person measures a day, not a routine [@frazis2012think_fix], which adds noise to individual outcomes but does not bias population means. Children under six are counted from the roster and assigned to a mother by a generational rule; the estimate that restricts to households with a single married woman of childbearing age is `r est_se(RB[[2]])`, but misassignment in households with several junior couples cannot be ruled out. The roster code for parents of the head does not distinguish the head's own parents from the spouse's parents, so for head-level mothers the maternal and paternal grandmother cannot be separated. Grandmother age proxies for health only imperfectly. The treatment is coresidence with a grandmother, not care she is observed to give to the mother's own child. Intervals are not adjusted for multiple comparisons across subgroups; individual subgroup estimates should be read as exploratory. Finally, the survey does not record which child a care episode is for, so in households with several young children the grandmother's recorded care may serve children other than the mother's. Future rounds that record the recipient of care, and surveys that follow the same families over the birth of a grandchild, would allow sharper tests.

## Conclusion

Diaries for every member of the household make it possible to measure directly what grandmothers and mothers do with the day in three-generation households. Identifying the generation above each mother correctly matters, because in patrilocal households the young mother lives in her parents-in-law's household and, unless the roster is read carefully, the head's wife would be counted as a mother rather than as the grandmother she is. With that identification, `r iff(!sub_child && !emp_up && !lfp_up, "the pooled association between a coresident grandmother and mothers' childcare or paid-work minutes is small and not robust, while grandmothers' own childcare is substantial and is associated with less free time and sleep for them, and with less domestic work, which the diaries cannot clearly trace to mothers", "coresident grandmothers are associated with different amounts of mothers' childcare and paid work, and grandmothers' own childcare is substantial")`. Family care in India involves the time of women of two generations whose terms depend on who the grandmother is and on how the household is arranged, and the time older women give is associated with less rest and leisure for them.
